items.question: What does Safety Tip #1 say about descending or terminating a pull-up in the R44 II?
options: Never push the cyclic forward to descend; always use the collective to initiate a descent
Push the cyclic forward gently, as in an airplane
Use only the pedals to control descent rate
Reduce throttle sharply to initiate a descent
items.explanation: Safety Tip #1 warns never to push the cyclic forward to descend or terminate a pull-up, as this may produce a low-G condition that can result in a main rotor blade striking the cabin; always use the collective to initiate a descent.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #1 (p.10-1)

items.question: According to Safety Tip #2, what should a pilot never intentionally allow in flight?
options: The oil temperature to enter the green arc
The fuel quantity to become so low that the low fuel warning light comes on
The carburetor heat to be applied above 3000 ft
The rotor RPM to remain in the green arc
items.explanation: Safety Tip #2 states a pilot should never intentionally allow the fuel quantity to become so low in flight that the low fuel warning light comes on.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #2 (p.10-1)

items.question: Why does Safety Tip #4 recommend turning the strobe light on before starting the engine and leaving it on until the rotors stop?
options: It improves engine cooling
It provides a warning to ground personnel, since the light is located near the tail rotor
It is required for night VFR only
It reduces electrical load on the battery
items.explanation: Safety Tip #4 explains the strobe light is located near the tail rotor and provides a warning to ground personnel while the rotors are turning; in-flight use of external lights during daylight is also recommended for collision avoidance.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #4 (p.10-1)

items.question: What does Safety Tip #9 warn can become dangerously low, and what is the consequence?
options: Fuel pressure — engine flameout
Rotor RPM — most hard landings are survivable if the rotor is not allowed to stall
Oil pressure — gearbox seizure
Manifold pressure — loss of climb performance
items.explanation: Safety Tip #9 states rotor RPM must never be allowed to become dangerously low; most hard landings will be survivable as long as the rotor is not allowed to stall.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #9 (p.10-2)

items.question: Why does Safety Tip #10 warn against downwind takeoffs or landings, especially at high altitude?
options: Downwind operations increase engine wear
The resulting loss of translational lift can cause the aircraft to settle into the ground or obstacles
Downwind operations exceed the crosswind limitation
It causes excessive tail rotor vibration
items.explanation: Safety Tip #10 warns that takeoffs or landings downwind, especially at high altitude, can cause a loss of translational lift resulting in the aircraft settling into the ground or obstacles.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #10 (p.10-2)

items.question: How can vortex ring state (VRS) best be avoided, per Safety Tip #11?
options: Reduce rate of descent before reducing airspeed
Reduce airspeed before reducing rate of descent
Increase collective immediately upon suspecting VRS
Maintain a steep, vertical descent profile at all times
items.explanation: Safety Tip #11 states vortex ring state can be avoided by always reducing rate of descent before reducing airspeed, since even maximum engine power may not stop the descent once VRS develops.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #11 (p.10-2)

items.question: According to Safety Tip #12, when is the helicopter stable on its landing gear?
options: Only when parked with the rotor brake engaged
As long as ground contact is made vertically or with the aircraft moving forward
Only at gross weights below 2000 lb
In any direction of ground contact
items.explanation: Safety Tip #12 states the helicopter is stable on its landing gear as long as ground contact is vertical or with the aircraft moving forward; contact while moving rearward or sideward can cause damage or rollover.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #12 (p.10-2)

items.question: What does Safety Tip #14 warn against using to slow the rotor during shutdown?
options: The rotor brake
Collective pitch, which can disengage the droop stop friction and allow blades to strike the tailcone
Cyclic control inputs
The governor override switch
items.explanation: Safety Tip #14 warns not to use collective pitch to slow the rotor during shutdown, since it produces lift on the blades that can disengage droop stop friction and allow blades to strike the tailcone.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #14 (p.10-3)

items.question: Why does Safety Tip #15 warn against landing in tall dry grass?
options: It reduces main rotor efficiency near the ground
The exhaust is low to the ground and very hot; a grass fire may be ignited
It increases the risk of dynamic rollover
It causes carburetor ice
items.explanation: Safety Tip #15 warns that the exhaust is low to the ground and very hot, and a grass fire may be ignited if the helicopter lands in tall dry grass.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #15 (p.10-3)

items.question: What does Safety Tip #17, on hydraulic-controlled aircraft, caution about abrupt control inputs?
options: They are not a concern because hydraulic boost absorbs the load
No feedback is felt in the flight controls, so the pilot may be unaware of high fatigue loads generated by abrupt inputs
They only matter above 100 KIAS
They primarily affect fuel consumption
items.explanation: Safety Tip #17 warns that with hydraulic controls, no feedback is felt, so the pilot may be unaware of the high fatigue loads generated by abrupt control inputs or accelerated maneuvers, which could cause premature, catastrophic component failure.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #17 (p.10-3)

items.question: What does Safety Tip #18 say about performing a magneto check in flight?
options: It should be done at least once per flight to verify magneto health
Never attempt a magneto check in flight; if a malfunction is suspected, leave the key in BOTH and land as soon as practical
It is only recommended above 3000 ft
It should be done immediately after any rough-running indication
items.explanation: Safety Tip #18 warns never to attempt a magneto check in flight, because grounding a malfunctioning magneto's opposite mag could stop the engine completely; if a malfunction is suspected, leave the key in BOTH and land as soon as practical.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #18 (p.10-3)

items.question: What does Safety Tip #19 warn about operating near the forward CG limit?
options: A fore-aft oscillation may develop during steep turns or autorotations as fuel burns and CG shifts forward
The helicopter becomes tail-heavy and prone to ground resonance
Autorotation entry becomes impossible
It only affects lateral, not longitudinal, handling
items.explanation: Safety Tip #19 warns that near the forward CG limit, a fore-aft oscillation may develop during steep turns or autorotations, since CG shifts forward as fuel is burned; returning to straight and level powered flight stops the oscillation.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #19 (p.10-3)

items.question: At higher altitudes (above 3000-4000 ft), how must RPM typically be controlled, per Safety Tip #13?
options: With the collective, since the throttle is frequently wide open and throttle/collective correlation is not effective
With the throttle only, since the collective has no correlation effect
RPM control becomes fully automatic via the governor
By reducing airspeed below Vy
items.explanation: Safety Tip #13 explains that at higher altitudes the throttle is frequently wide open and RPM must be controlled with the collective, since throttle/collective correlation is not effective and governor response is fairly slow under these conditions.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: SAFETY TIPS #13 (p.10-3)

items.question: Under 14 CFR §61.56 and §61.57 recurrency requirements, what does the PILOT KNOWLEDGE AND PROFICIENCY section of Section 10 recommend?
options: Periodic study and recurrent training beyond minimum regulatory requirements to maintain proficiency
Recurrent training is only necessary for commercial operators
Only limitations need periodic review, not procedures
Proficiency review is optional if total flight hours exceed 500
items.explanation: PILOT KNOWLEDGE AND PROFICIENCY states that in addition to complying with 14 CFR §61.56 and §61.57 recurrency requirements, all pilots should keep their knowledge current through periodic study and recurrent training, with emphasis on listed review topics.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: PILOT KNOWLEDGE AND PROFICIENCY (p.10-4)

items.question: According to PILOT KNOWLEDGE AND PROFICIENCY, low-G training should be conducted how?
options: Practiced in flight under instructor supervision only
Knowledge based only — never practiced or demonstrated in flight
Practiced solo after 100 hours of experience
Only demonstrated in a full-motion simulator, never discussed
items.explanation: The recommended review topics note that low-G should never be practiced or demonstrated in flight; low-G training should be knowledge based only.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: PILOT KNOWLEDGE AND PROFICIENCY (p.10-5)

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-9, what is the most effective way to stop a dynamic rollover once it has started?
options: Applying full opposite cyclic
Quickly applying down collective
Increasing throttle to regain rotor authority
Applying opposite pedal
items.explanation: SN-9 explains that once a dynamic rollover starts, opposite cyclic alone cannot stop it because the thrust vector follows the aircraft as it rolls; quickly applying down collective is the most effective way to stop a dynamic rollover.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-9

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-9, what liftoff technique helps avoid dynamic rollover?
options: A rapid, single-motion liftoff to clear the ground quickly
A two-step liftoff: pull in just enough collective to be light on the skids and feel for equilibrium, then gently lift off
Applying full collective immediately from a hover check
Lifting off with cyclic displaced away from any nearby obstacle
items.explanation: SN-9 recommends always using a two-step liftoff: first pull in just enough collective to be light on the skids and feel for equilibrium, then gently lift the helicopter into the air, to avoid a skid catching on an obstacle and causing dynamic rollover.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-9

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-10, what must a pilot do first when rotor RPM decays, regardless of the cause?
options: Investigate the cause before taking any control action
Roll on throttle and lower the collective simultaneously to recover RPM, as a conditioned reflex
Raise the collective to arrest the rate of descent
Enter a steep bank to reduce airspeed
items.explanation: SN-10 states that no matter what causes low rotor RPM, the pilot must first roll on throttle and lower the collective simultaneously to recover RPM before investigating the problem — it must be a conditioned reflex.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-10

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-11, how should the rotor be reloaded to stop a roll during a low-G condition?
options: Immediately apply a gentle aft cyclic movement, avoiding large cyclic inputs
Apply full lateral cyclic opposite the roll direction
Lower the collective sharply
Apply forward cyclic to regain airspeed first
items.explanation: SN-11 states the rotor must be reloaded before lateral cyclic can stop any roll; to reload the rotor, immediately apply a gentle aft cyclic movement, but avoid any large cyclic inputs. Low-G pushovers should never be intentionally demonstrated.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-11

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-15, when should a pilot always land to refuel, to avoid fuel exhaustion?
options: Before the main tank fuel gage reads less than 1/4 full
Only once the low fuel warning light illuminates
Whenever the hourmeter shows more than 2 hours since last fill
There is no specific recommended threshold
items.explanation: SN-15 recommends always landing to refuel before the main tank fuel gage reads less than 1/4 full, and never allowing fuel quantity to become so low that the low fuel warning light comes on.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-15

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-16, what is the recommended technique for crossing power lines?
options: Fly directly over the towers, since the wires themselves may be invisible until too close
Fly under the wires where they are easiest to see
Fly parallel to the line at a safe lateral distance
Descend low enough to identify the exact wire height first
items.explanation: SN-16 recommends flying directly over the towers when crossing power lines, watching for towers since the wires (especially smaller grounding wires) will often not be seen in time, and always maintaining at least 500 ft AGL except during takeoff and landing.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-16

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-19, what minimum altitude does Robinson recommend to avoid the hazards of flying low over water?
options: Maintain 500 ft AGL whenever possible, and avoid maneuvers over water below 200 ft AGL
Maintain 1000 ft AGL at all times over water
There is no altitude guidance for flight over water
Maintain 100 ft AGL to preserve depth perception
items.explanation: SN-19 recommends maintaining 500 ft AGL whenever possible and avoiding maneuvers over water below 200 ft AGL, since calm or choppy water surfaces interfere with normal depth perception.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-19

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-22, what rule of thumb helps avoid vortex ring state (VRS)?
options: Never allow airspeed to be less than 30 knots until rate of descent is less than 300 feet per minute
Keep airspeed above 60 knots at all times during descent
Maintain a constant rate of descent regardless of airspeed
Increase collective as soon as vibration is felt
items.explanation: SN-22 gives the rule: never allow your airspeed to be less than 30 knots until your rate of descent is less than 300 feet per minute, to avoid vortex ring state.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-22

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-28, what does it mean if the clutch light flickers or does not go out within 10 seconds?
options: It is normal drive belt re-tensioning and can be ignored
It can indicate a belt or bearing failure, requiring the clutch circuit breaker to be pulled and power reduced
It only indicates a low battery charge
It means the governor has disengaged
items.explanation: SN-28 states that while a brief clutch light illumination (3-6 seconds) for belt re-tensioning is normal, a flickering light or one that does not go out within 10 seconds can indicate a belt or bearing failure; the pilot should pull the clutch circuit breaker, reduce power, and make a precautionary landing.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-28

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-32, what airspeed range is recommended when flying in moderate or greater turbulence?
options: A slower-than-normal cruise speed of 60-70 knots
Maximum cruise speed to minimize time in turbulence
Vne minus 10 knots
Autorotation minimum speed of 40 knots
items.explanation: SN-32 recommends reducing power and using a slower-than-normal cruise speed of 60-70 knots in turbulence, since low-G mast bumping is significantly less likely at lower airspeeds.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-32

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-33, what is the maximum allowable inboard deflection of the drive belts, checked with the clutch disengaged?
options: 0.5 inches (1.3 cm)
1.5 inches (4 cm)
3.0 inches (7.6 cm)
There is no specified maximum
items.explanation: SN-33 states that with the clutch disengaged, deflecting the belts inboard just above the fan scroll should show a maximum of 1.5 inches (4 cm) deflection; if belts deflect further, the belt tension actuator must be adjusted before flight.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-33

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-36, what should a pilot always confirm before increasing RPM above 80% during liftoff?
options: That the carb heat is fully off
That the governor is on
That the fuel valve is on
That the mixture guard is removed
items.explanation: SN-36 recommends always confirming the governor is on before increasing RPM above 80%, verifying the governor stabilizes RPM near the top of the green arc, and maintaining a relaxed grip on the throttle to avoid overriding the governor and causing an overspeed.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-36

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-38, what is the maximum recommended number of consecutive practice autorotations, to limit training accidents?
options: No more than 3 or 4 consecutive autorotations
No more than 10 consecutive autorotations
There is no recommended limit as long as fuel allows
Only 1 per training flight
items.explanation: SN-38 recommends limiting practice to no more than 3 or 4 consecutive autorotations to maintain instructor focus and minimize student fatigue, since a high percentage of training accidents occur after many consecutive autorotations.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-38

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-38, what four parameters make up the instructor's "100 Foot Decision Check" before continuing a practice autorotation below 100 feet AGL?
options: Rotor RPM ~100%, airspeed 60-70 KIAS stabilized, descent rate usually below 1500 ft/min, turns completed
Rotor RPM ~90%, airspeed 40-50 KIAS, descent rate below 500 ft/min, engine at idle
Airspeed only, checked at 200 feet AGL
Manifold pressure, carb heat setting, mixture position, and fuel flow
items.explanation: SN-38's 100 Foot Decision Check requires: rotor RPM approximately 100%, stabilized airspeed between 60 and 70 KIAS, stabilized rate of descent usually less than 1500 ft/min, and turns (if any) completed, before descending below 100 feet AGL (200 feet or higher above 4000 ft density altitude).
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-38

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-42, what is the correct understanding of "unanticipated yaw" on Robinson helicopters?
options: It is always caused by loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE), meaning the tail rotor stalled

It is usually caused by a pilot's failure to apply proper pedal inputs in gusty or crosswind conditions, not true LTE, since Robinson tail rotors have more authority and are unlikely to experience LTE
It only occurs above 40 KIAS
It cannot occur if the governor is functioning normally
items.explanation: SN-42 clarifies that unanticipated yaw is usually a pilot's failure to apply proper pedal inputs in response to strong or gusty winds, not true loss of tail rotor effectiveness — Robinson tail rotors are designed with more authority than many other helicopters and are unlikely to experience LTE.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-42

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-44, how many total helicopter hours (including hours in type) should a newly-rated pilot accumulate before carrying passengers?
options: 50 total hours, no in-type requirement
100 total hours helicopter experience, including 20 hours pilot-in-command in type
10 total hours in any helicopter
There is no recommended minimum
items.explanation: SN-44 recommends newly-rated helicopter pilots not carry passengers until accumulating 100 total hours of helicopter experience, including 20 hours pilot-in-command in type after receiving their helicopter rating.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-44

items.question: Per Safety Notice SN-30, which cabin door configuration is specifically prohibited to prevent loose objects from being sucked out toward the tail rotor?
options: Flying with the left door removed (only the right door should be removed for ventilation)
Flying with both front doors installed
Flying with the aft doors removed
There is no door configuration restriction
items.explanation: SN-30 states a pilot should never fly with a left door removed, and should remove only the right door for ventilation, as part of preventing loose objects from being sucked out and striking the tail rotor.
references: R44 II POH Sec 10: Safety Notice SN-30
